newsitem.title: USA: Grunge fad will get less space under the tree this year.
newsitem.headline: Grunge fad will get less space under the tree this year.

text.p: Parents longing for the "grunge" fad to find its way to the bottom of the sock drawer will get some relief this Christmas.

Retailers are stocking more colourful and better-fitting clothes modelled after 1970s styles. That means boxes under the Christmas tree will be filled with corduroy jumpers, polyester blouses and hip-huggers instead of baggy, bottom-revealing jeans, retailing experts said.

Target, the Minneapolis-based discount store giant that is popular among teens, has sold a lot of stretchy velour tops this fall. They were popular last year, but this year chocolate brown has outsold black for the first time.
"Brown is the new black," said Robyn Waters, chief trend watcher for Target, a division of Dayton Hudson Corp. "The new neutral colour family is the browns."
Lighter, clingier merchandise has taken the place of oversized, bulky flannel shirts and vintage furniture at many clothing and housewares chains.

"I think everyone has suffered enough with gold-plated this and brass-and-gold-leaf that," said Kenneth Wingard, director of retail merchandise at the Pottery Barn. "We're getting away from the shabby chic. We're calling it soft modern."
Consumers who shunned lavish furnishings and high-priced fashion after the recession ended early this decade now are more comfortable making a statement, experts said.
In the teen market, which often influences adult fashion, the grunge look has evolved into a retro fad with go-go boots, knit shirts and tops marked with mock-Adidas athletic stripes.
"This is a different look than the Generation X teen wore," said Maria Medaris O'Shea, who follows youth-oriented retailers for Alex. Brown & Sons Inc. in Baltimore.
With Generation Xers, the look was "anti-fashion" and down-and-out, she said. Teens these days are sporting more feminine and stylish duds.

At Pacific Sunwear of California Inc., a casual apparel retailer that's popular among teens, the "sagger" pant has not disappeared, the company said. It's been modified to an oversized slack with a 30-inch leg opening that flares but doesn't bunch up under the heel.

"People are saying oversized is dead. It's not dead," said Timothy Harmon, Pacific Sunwear's senior vice president of merchandising. Fashion "is a little more irreverant now. There are sparks of colour that we haven't seen in the past."

Even mainstream retailer Nordstrom Inc. has noticed the change. Colours are mellower and styles are more flirtatious. Junior customers are shopping for bell bottoms, snug sweaters and long, flared jackets.
"As an overall statement, grunge is less strong," said Nordstrom spokeswoman Amy Jones. "Femininity is a trend not only in silhouettes but fabrics as well."

The retro look probably won't appeal to parents, who like the clean cut of khaki pants and navy blue sweaters, observers said. But teens today are less likely than ever to wear something just to please their parents.
"Teens normally conform to one another and not to the outside world," said O'Shea of Alex. Brown.

Pacific Sunwear, which does a lot of business in cash, knows its core customers are teens themselves. While the customer base shifts toward plastic-toting parents during the holidays, the stuff that kids want doesn't change.
"Most kids who are 15 or 16, they know their parents have an opinion," Pacific Sunwear's Harmon said. "And most parents admit that if they buy something their kids don't like, it won't be worn."
